opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I valued most was the freedom to make every design decision end to end, and to own the consequences of those decisions. When you build something alone, especially in the early stage, there's no one to hand the hard parts off to. If the compiler has a bug, it's your bug. If the API feels awkward, you feel that awkwardness every single day because you're also the first user. That's painful sometimes, but it forces a kind of coherence. The language frontend, the intermediate representation, the optimization passes, the backends for CPU and GPU, the examples and documentation, they all came from one mental model, so they fit together in a way that's hard to achieve when a system is designed by committee from day one.

The second thing was speed of iteration. During my PhD, I could have an idea in the morning, say a new way to handle sparse data structures, prototype it in the afternoon, and by night I'd know whether it worked on a real physics simulation. There's no meeting, no alignment process. For a research project, that loop is incredibly valuable, because most ideas fail, and you want them to fail fast and cheaply.

And honestly, I valued the deep learning it gave me personally. Before Taichi, I was mostly a graphics person writing simulation code. Building a compiler on my own pushed me into areas I didn't know well, like LLVM, memory hierarchies, GPU programming models, and language design. You only really understand a system when you've had to build and debug the whole stack yourself.

That said, I don't want to romanticize it too much. Working alone also has clear limits. At some point Taichi had users who needed things I simply didn't have the bandwidth for, and the project became much better once more people joined and the community grew. So I'd say the solo phase was valuable for establishing a clear vision and a solid foundation, but a project like this can only reach its potential when it stops being one person's project.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what I valued most was the freedom to make every decision myself, and to live with the consequences of those decisions very directly.

When I started Taichi during my PhD, it wasn't really a product. It was a tool I needed. I was doing physical simulation research, writing things like MPM solvers, and I was spending maybe eighty percent of my time fighting CUDA and data structures instead of thinking about the physics. So the first version was really just me scratching my own itch. Nobody told me what the language should look like, which meant I could try strange ideas, throw them away the next week, and nobody was affected but me.

That kind of tight loop is something you lose once a project has users and collaborators. Early on, I could change the whole frontend in a weekend because I had an intuition it would be cleaner. Later, every change has to go through discussion, backward compatibility, documentation. That's healthy for a mature project, but it's slow. Doing it alone at the beginning let me converge on the core design very quickly.

The other thing is that building the whole stack yourself forces you to understand it end to end. The frontend, the IR, the optimizations, the backends, the memory layouts for sparse data structures. I couldn't hand any piece off, so I had to learn all of it. That was painful at times, but it gave me a mental model of the entire system that I still rely on. When someone reports a bug today, I can often guess where it is because I remember writing that part at two in the morning.

And honestly, there was a personal side. Working alone on something for a long time teaches you to keep going when there's no external validation. For the first year or two, almost nobody used Taichi. I had to decide, on my own, that it was worth continuing. Going through that made me much more confident later when we built a team and a company around it, because I knew the foundation was something I believed in, not something I'd been told to believe in.

astra-6.text: What I valued most was the freedom to explore. Working on Taichi on my own meant I could follow an idea, try it out, and change direction without having to coordinate every decision. It also pushed me to think about the whole system—how the language should feel to someone using it and how the implementation could make it efficient. That connection between design and implementation was really satisfying.
